issues.legal_issue: Agrarian reform provisions that reduce landholders’ retained agricultural land, protect cultivators’ interests, and redistribute surplus agricultural land to landless tillers are protected from constitutional challenge when they have a close nexus to the common-good objective of distributing material resources.
material_facts: The challenged amendments reduced the agricultural land that landholders could retain and regulated the rights of cultivators working the land.

The legislation took surplus agricultural land from landholders and made it available to landless tillers, while leaving landholders land within the prescribed ceiling and not taking their homestead lands or buildings.
The amendments were directed at distributing agricultural land, a material resource, for the common good.
issues.conclusion: The challenged provisions were protected by Article 31C because they gave effect to Article 39(b), and the constitutional challenges to them failed.
issues.legal_principle: Article 39(b) concerns distribution of the community’s material resources to serve the common good. Distribution is not confined to a literal division; it includes allocation, allotment, classification, and apportionment. A broad approach applies when assessing the required nexus between legislation and Article 39(b). Where that nexus exists, Article 31C protects the legislation from challenges based on the fundamental rights it covers. The Court relied on Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India, Waman Rao v. Union of India, Sanjeev Coke Manufacturing Co. v. Bharat Coking Coal Ltd., State of Tamil Nadu v. L. Abu Kavur Bai, State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy, Sri Sri Kalimata Thakurani v. Union of India, and Sasanka Sekhar Maity v. Union of India.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_ref: Landholders brought a constitutional challenge to legislation reforming agricultural landholding.
predicates.surplus_agricultural_land_taken_from_lan: The legislation took agricultural land above the amount landholders could retain.
predicates.agricultural_land_allocated_to_landless_: The legislation allocated agricultural land to landless people who cultivated it.
predicates.close_nexus_to_common_good: The legislation’s land-distribution measures were closely connected to serving the common good.

issues.definition: When landholders challenge agrarian reform that takes surplus agricultural land and allocates it to landless tillers, a close connection between that distribution and the common good means the challenged provisions are protected from fundamental-rights challenge.

issues.legal_issue: A requirement that a landholder reside near the land for most of the year and derive the principal source of income from it is valid where it supports personal cultivation and the legislation serves the common-good objective of distributing material resources.
material_facts: The challenged provision required the landholder or a family member to reside for the greater part of the year in the locality where the land was situated and required the principal source of income to come from that land.
The provision was intended to ensure that a landholder cultivating the land gave it attention rather than remaining an absentee landholder pursuing other occupations.
The provision formed part of legislation directed at distributing agricultural resources for the common good.
issues.conclusion: The residence requirement was not an impermissible ground for invalidating the legislation; Article 31C barred the fundamental-rights challenge, and the requirement was also reasonable and beneficial to cultivation.
issues.legal_principle: Where legislation has a close nexus to the objectives in Article 39(b), Article 31C protects it from the covered fundamental-rights challenges. A requirement that a cultivator reside near the land for most of the year can further effective cultivation, agricultural production, and equitable distribution. The Court relied on Article 39(b), Article 31C, and its reasoning in Sri Sri Kalimata Thakurani v. Union of India.

issues.definition: When landholders challenge agrarian reform containing a residence and income condition that supports personal cultivation, the condition is valid and protected from fundamental-rights challenge if the reform is closely connected to serving the common good.
